description.narrative:
Overall goal Scaling up gender transformative approached in advocacy, accountability culture and partnership effectiveness to advance MEA regional impact and sustainability. The Strategic Plan 20142027 has three strategic areas and in total seven objectives:
Strategic area 1: Advocacy
Objective 1: Position MEA as a leading male engagement movement in the region within its thematic areas by mobilising collective voices and actions to influence policies and legal reforms.
Objective 2: Scale up gender transformative advocacy through capacity strengthening MEA's network and strategic partners to advance feminist approaches and principles.
Strategic area 2: Accountability
Objective 3: Improve systems and structures to operationalize and popularise existing MEA accountability mechanism for effective collaboration responsiveness and functionality of the movement.
Objective 4: Advance MEA's joint actions an initiatives through capacity strengthening of partners utilising country and regional channels to achieve MEA's goals
Strategic area 3: Partnerships
Objective 5: Implement capacity strengthening initiatives on gender transformative approached including MenEngage Africa Training Initiative (MATI)
Objective 6: Identify strengthen and maintain strategic partnerships for collaboration across MEA thematic areas at national, regional and global levels.
Objective 7: Contribute to resource mobilization for the sustainability of the MEA network

Men Engage Africa är ett av globala Men Engage Alliansens regionala nätverk. Men Engage Africa nätverket består av 22 nationella Men Engage Africa nätverk (Botswana, Burundi, Kamerun, Etiopien, Demokratiska Republiken Kongo, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini) med medlemmar på nationell nivå. Men Engage nätverket fokuserar hur maskulinitetsnormer är formade, hur de påverkar samhället, relationer och individer. Kärnan i nätverkets arbete är att bidra till jämställdhet mellan könen, förbättra sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter (SRHR), och minska förekomsten av könsbaserat våld genom att engagera pojkar och män genom "gender transformation" - metoder som utmanar och förändrar negativa manlighetsnormer. Nätverket har etablerat sig som en ledande aktör på global, regional och nationell nivå inom detta fält sedan 2009.

The contribution is a project support to Sonke Gender Justice for the implementation of Men Engage Africa's Strategic Plan 2019-2024. The core of Men Engage Africa's work is qualitative work on men and masculinity within women’s rights, SRHR and gender justice for all with the aim to contributing to Gender Equality.

description.narrative:
Advocacy
MenEngage Africa (MEA) continued to work to uphold MEA as a leading male engagement movement in the region by scaling up gender transformative advocacy, below are a few examples of accomplishments in the reporting period.
MEA actively engaged in the Beijing 30 review, by co-developing a multi-country report that assessed progress on implementing the SDGs in Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Africa, and the DRC. The report was launched at CSW69 and highlighted achievements and persistent gaps in womens health, violence against women and womens participation in conflict. It underscored the critical importance of engaging men and boys as partners in achieving gender equality. MEA also worked for stronger civil society participation, through hybrid models of engagement, improved data collection, and closer coordination between CSW, the UPR, and treaty bodies which contributed in shifting the conversation toward accountability and inclusion, with a sharper focus on emerging challenges such as artificial intelligence. The process is expected to produce more ambitious and action-oriented commitments, driving tangible progress at national and regional levels, closing gender gaps, and strengthening trust in multilateral systems.
MEA further contributed in shaping the first binding continental legal framework to end violence against women and girls, embedding prevention standards, accountability mechanisms, and a platform for sharing best practices across Member States in the African Union Convention on Eliminating Violence Against Women and Girls (AUCEVAWG). By engaging in AU-led consultations they ensured that both male engagement and the lived realities of African women were reflected throughout the drafting process. A key contribution was their input into the AU Positive Masculinities Paper, one of the foundational documents for the Convention, which helped establish a more holistic approach to gender equality by recognising men and boys as partners in transformation. The advocacy directly influenced the inclusion of positive masculinity as a guiding principle in Article 6 of the Convention, which means that they have contributed to concrete legal and policy outcomes that will shape gender justice efforts across Africa for years to come.
MEA partners have further continued to use research and knowledge generation to strengthen advocacy, document best practices, and influence policy across the region. The State of Fathers Report in Zimbabwe, developed in collaboration with SAfAIDS and GIZ, and which highlights how unequal unpaid care responsibilities contribute to gender inequality and GBV, while providing evidence to inform community interventions and national policy. In Uganda, the Power to Youth programme has demonstrated how Human-Centred Design (HCD) empowers youth to co-create innovative, context-specific solutions, such as increasing contraceptive uptake in Kalangala (Uganda). MEA partners also published the study Analysis of Ugandas Anti-Homosexuality Act and its Implications on Access to Healthcare Services by the LGBTQI Communities, which shows how punitive laws undermine public health, human rights, and gender justice. The initiatives demonstrate how MEA leverages participatory research and evidence to amplify voices and inform programming to contribute to systemic change.
MEA further continued to build and mobilise a coalition of civil society organisations across its 24-country networks. A series of capacity-building webinars aimed to strengthen members advocacy skills, particularly in intersectionality and disability-inclusive SRHR. For example, the webinar on Enhancing SRHR through Intersectionality (co-hosted by IPAS Ethiopia and partners in Uganda and Malawi) deepened participants' ability to design inclusive programs responsive to women with disabilities. Similarly, the webinar on the Africa Disability Protocol and SRHR, held in October 2024 and facilitated by Sonke and the Centre for Human Rights at the University of Pretoria, engaged 50 participants in exploring how to drive inclusive SRHR reforms. Outcomes included commitments to push for national ratification, improve accessibility in health facilities, and involve people with disabilities in policy design.
MEA together with partners including UNFPA ESARO, Equality Now, Akina Mama wa Afrika and the Power to Youth Consortium, continued thew work to advocate for the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) in the fight against Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) by granting permission to two lawmakers to introduce a Bill seeking to eliminate the harmful practice across the region. The work aimed to sustain the long and costly legislative process at EALA. They managed to ensure funding and technical support for consultation meetings with legislators in Kampala (Nov 2024) and Nairobi (Feb 2025 followed by a drafting and validation meeting in Nairobi (March 2025) that incorporated CSO input. The groundwork culminated in the proposing of the Bill at EALA in April 2025 which was a major regional victory against harmful practices. The Bill directly addresses cross-border FGM and leverages male engagement as a strategy to end harmful practices and advance SRHR. In the next phase, country-level consultations before presentation to Heads of State for accession, will rely heavily on MEA networks, which are present in seven of the eight EAC member states. This positions MEA and its partners not only as key drivers of the Bills success but also as essential actors in ensuring its domestication and implementation across the region.
Accountability
MEA has continued to hold convenings at both national and regional levels. The national and regional Annual General Meetings (AGMs) has been serving as key platforms to review progress, adopt accountability resolutions and refine strategic priorities. Youth steering committees were established across multiple regions, and the election participation rates in the Youth AGM as well as the other and AGMs remained high at an attendance rate of over 70%. Steady feedback loops and responsive governance was strengthened through the quarterly regional and national steering committee meetings which brought together coordinators and youth representatives from across the region.
Partnerships
In the period from January 2024 to June 2025, MEA conducted a partner mapping alongside governance cleanup and reaffirmation, with networks documenting their active and compliant members, and with Secretariat systems transitioning toward a centralised database system tracking network membership status and MOUs across MEA countries. They piloted MATI as a hybrid flagship. The 2024 MATI anchored the reporting periods deep-dive on capacity strengthening, with the cohort on Building Feminist Peace in Africa. It as a four-week online course, which was then followed by an inperson intensive session in Nairobi, assembling 25 activists from 18 countries in a feminist, practice-to policy pedagogy that linked WPS, positive masculinities, and Gender Transformative Approaches (hereinafter GTA). According to MEA the alumni immediately translated their learning into action through region-based teams, public webinars, and country-level awareness sessions. In partnership with the University of Iceland, MEA initiated the development of the first self-paced MATI online module on engaging men and boys in SRHR. To complement the MATI training, Sonke and its partners developed practical tools, such as the Step-by-Step Guide on Gender-Transformative Approaches in SRHR Programming, which was tested with implementers in Uganda, Kenya, Senegal, and Malawi. The guide aimed to move GTA from concept to routine program practice and standardise the documentation of promising approaches.
MEA further continued to collaborate with a number of different actors such as WILPF, Nala Feminist Collective, Global Fund for Children (GFC) and Save the Children. They further sought government partnerships to move beyond external advocacy with the focus on co-design. In Zimbabwe, collaboration with the Ministry of Womens Affairs on a National Strategy for Male Engagement secured formal recognition and access to policy processes. In Eswatini, cooperation with the Deputy Prime Ministers Office on International Mens Day established high-visibility channels for promoting positive masculinity and preventing GBV. Led by Sonke, MenCare in Africa, now links approximately 50 organisations in 18 countries and attracts co-funders, including ADA, GIZ, Save the Children and Generation Gender, to support gender transformative approaches that provide donors and civil society with a mechanism for coordinated care-economy and fatherhood work.
Resource mobilisation
Between January 2024 and June 2025, the MenEngage Africa (MEA) resource mobilisation strategy has focused on maintaining growth through diversification and system strengthening in a tougher donor landscape. Building on the momentum of the previous funding cycle, MEA entered 2024 with a broad base of established donors, including Sida (CSO-unit), the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, NORAD, and the Ford Foundation, while also leveraging programme brands like MenCare to attract renewed and new partners such as ADA, GIZ, Pivot, Save the Children, and Generation Gender. Although aggregate funding levels did not climb as steeply as in the 20192023 period, MEA sustained a robust portfolio through strategic coalition bids, rolling concept notes, and evidence-driven advocacy that positioned it well in a context of shrinking civic space and multiple grant closures. Notably, 2024 saw continuity financing at country level, with partners in Namibia securing new funding support from the Australian Embassy after ADAs close-out, demonstrating stronger local ownership of MEAs brand.
Forwardig of funds
MEA managed a portfolio of over 50 sub-grants between the reporting period from January 2024 to June 2025, with structured compliance and built-in support such as monthly/quarterly reviews against subgrant terms, country level monitoring and remedial action where needed. The MEA subgrant model further mitigated common risks such as slow donor approvals, reporting delays, fragile-context access constraints, and financial volatility). MEA equipped partners to institutionalise solutions such as financial risk policies and variance tracking through the utilisation of standard templates and clear
workflow calendars. At the same time, MEA coordinated exits or handovers when funding was discontinued (e.g., USAIDs halt to South Sudan) and provided endorsements to support networks in sustaining their operations post-grant.
